newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan plantation labour seen losing clout.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan plantation labour seen losing clout.

text.p: Sri Lanka's biggest estate labour union could lose formidable bargaining power after members voted against the government in last week's local polls, analysts said on Monday.

"The CWC (Ceylon Workers' Congress) is likely to have less bargaining power, for instance, to win wage hikes, than before," said Sene Seneviratne, director-general of the Planters' Association of Ceylon.
The CWC has won wage hikes in the past by threatening strikes that could badly disrupt the plantations industry, traditionally the bedrock of the Indian Ocean island's economy.
The union, made up mainly of minority Tamil plantation workers of Indian origin, is considered politically powerful.
Its leadership has used the union's estimated 400,000 members as a bloc vote to help one or another of Sri Lanka's two main political parties at elections.

But it failed to deliver its bloc vote to the ruling People's Alliance (PA) coalition in Friday's election despite calls by CWC leader Saumyamoorthy Thondaman, Minister of Rural Industries in the PA cabinet.
Instead, CWC supporters voted in large numbers for the opposition United National Party (UNP), the party they had backed for 17 years until it was ousted by the PA in 1994.

The PA swept to a landslide victory in the poll, winning 194 of the 238 local bodies at stake. The UNP won only 43, mainly in the central hills where large numbers of Tamils of Indian origin work on tea estates.
Thondaman, long a UNP cabinet minister before switching sides after its 1994 defeat, was quoted on Sunday as saying the government failed to fulfil the workers' aspirations.
"Thondaman is not needed by anybody," UNP member of parliament Anura Bandaranaike told a news conference on Sunday. "He has not delivered to the government and we won without him."
The CWC is currently nearing a deal on a collective agreement with management firms running Sri Lanka's tea, rubber and coconut plantations.
Management firms already have a deal with the union to freeze wages up to December 1997, as a prelude to the collective agreement.
Seneviratne said Thondaman was a very astute leader who had always bounced back from difficult situations.
"It remains to be seen whether Thondaman's overall control of plantation labour had dropped," he said.
"He has done very well by his people. Even in our talks on the collective agreement he has been fairly reasonable saying he wants industrial peace and that there is a need to improve productivity."

Professor S. Sandarasegaran of Colombo University said that although the CWC members may not support the political actions of their leaders as demonstrated by last week's poll, they could still work together on labour issues.
"They may support the CWC when it comes to labour issues like wage hikes," he said.
Industry analysts said estate workers were dissatisfied with the CWC leadership and confused by the opportunistic way Thondaman switched sides.
Sandarasegaran said a new middle class had emerged in recent years in the Indian Tamil community, which had been neglected for decades despite their contribution to the economy.
